technical-data.invention-title: ARTICLES COATED WITH ABRASION RESISTANT COATING
ARTICLES REVETUS D'UN REVETEMENT RESISTANT A L'ABRASION

abstract.p: A coating composition includes a cured base coat (12) of polyurethane-containing resin covered by a cured top coat (14) of a silicon-containing resin. The top coat resin is applied in an uncured state to the base coat, the two resins are thereafter heated to at least 140 F, and thereafter the top coat resin is cured to produce the coating composition. A clean metal surface (11) is coated with the coating composition by applying uncured base coat (12) resin to the metal surface (11), curing the base coat resin, and thereafter applying the top coat (14) as described above.

L'invention concerne une composition de revêtement comprenant une couche de base durcie (12) de résine de polyuréthanne recouverte d'une couche supérieure durcie (14) de résine de silicium. La couche supérieure non durcie est appliquée sur la couche de base et les deux résines sont ensuite chauffées à au moins 140 F. La résine de la couche supérieure est alors durcie afin d'obtenir la composition de revêtement. On recouvre une surface métallique propre (11) avec la composition de revêtement, par l'application d'une couche de fond non durcie (12) de résine sur la surface métallique (11), par durcissement de la résine de la couche de base, puis par l'application de la couche supérieure (14) comme décrit ci-dessus.

description.p: ARTICLES COATED WITH ABRASION RESISTANT COATING ABRASION RESISTANT COATING COMPOSITIONS,
METHODS FOR MAKING THEM. AND ARTICLES COATED WITH THEM
CROSS-REFERENCE TO RELATED APPLICATIONS This application claims inventions disclosed in co-pending provisional Application No.
60/126.587 filed March 26. 1999 and co-pending provisional Application No. 60/147,328 filed August 5. 1999.
BACKGROUND OF THE INVENTION This invention relates to abrasion-resistant coating compositions, methods for making them, and articles coated with them.

More particularly, the invention provides an improved silicon-containing cured synthetic resin coating composition which forms a protective, abrasion resistant coating. Such coating compositions are sometimes referred to as silicone hard coat resins, or organo-polysiloxanes, such as the compounds produced by the condensation of hydroxy organosilicon compounds formed by the hydrolysis of organosilicon halides. The preferred silicon-containing coating compositions include products which combine colloidal silica with various acryloxy or glycidoxy functional compounds, such as acryloxy or glycidoxy functional silanes, or non-silyl acrylates.

Transparent abrasion-resistant coatings made from silicon-containing synthetic resins have been used to coat transparent plastics which do not shatter or are more resistant to shattering than glass, but which are subject to scratching and marring due to everyday contact with abrasives such as dust, cleaning equipment, and ordinary weathering. However, the application of these prior art coating compositions to metal surfaces has met with little success because of inadequate adhesion between the metal and the cured resin.
SUMMARY OF THE INVENTION

This invention provides a silicon-containing cured synthetic resin coating composition which bonds firmly to metal surfaces to provide superior protection from abrasion and chemical attack. The coating composition of the invention includes a base coat layer of cured polyurethane-containing resin which bonds strongly to the metal surface to be protected. A top coat layer of uncured silicon-containing synthetic resin is deposited on the cured layer of polyurethane-containing resin, and heated to create a strong interlinking between the silicon-containing synthetic resin and the layer of polyurethane-containing resin. Thereafter, the silicon-containing synthetic resin is cured by heat, actinic radiation such as UV light, or particle radiation such as electron beam. The final silicon-containing cured synthetic resin coating composition can be clear or pigmented. For example, the polyurethane-containing resin can include pigment or metallic particles for decorative effect.
Practically any kind of metal surface which has been adequately cleaned can be coated in accordance with this invention. The polyurethane-containing layer can be any of the well-known polyurethane coating compositions, or blends of polyurethane and acrylic resin. The layer of polyurethane or polyurethane/acrylic mixture is coated onto a clean metal surface by any of the suitable, well-known and commercially available processes, such as spraying or electrodeposition.

DESCRIPTION OF THE INVENTION The Polvurethane-Containing Resin

As used herein, the terms "polyurethane resin" and ''polyurethane-containing resin" include resins which are either all polyurethane, polyurethane which includes epoxy groups, or an acrylic-polyurethane copolymer as described below, or a mixture of those resins.
My presently preferred process for electrodeposition of a base coat of a polyurethane-containing resin on metal surfaces is disclosed in ClearClad Coatings, Inc."s

Installation and Operation Manual (Release No. 2.0, Manual Series No: 1 192, Copyrighted 1997 by ClearClad Coatings, Inc.). A copy of the Manual is attached as Appendix 1. The electrodeposition process described in the Manual is referred to as electrophoretic coating. The process deposits a cross-linked organic polyurethane-containing lacquer coating to any metal with proper treatment as described in the Manual. The base coat of the polyurethane-containing resin can be clear or colored (with pigment), translucent or opaque, and has a substantially uniform thickness over the coated surface, usually in the range of 1-100 microns (.00004"-.0040").

For coating aluminum and magnesium surfaces, I prefer to use ClearClad LCX® polyurethane electrocoat enamel supplied by ClearClad Coatings, Inc., and which is described in the manual on page 48. That type of polyurethane electrocoat enamel is described in U.S.

Patent Nos. 3,922.253, 3,947,338. and 4.241.200, which are incorporated herein by reference. The polyurethane electrocoating composition is produced by reacting an isocyanate-terminated prepolymer with a minor amount of peroxide to provide a polyurethane polymer blocked with pendant peroxide groups, and then co-reacting acrylic monomers with minor amounts of other ethylenically unsaturated monomers in the presence of the preformed polyurethane peroxide polymer to provide polyurethane copolymer with those monomers. The resulting polyurethane acrylic block copolymer can also contain carboxyl or amine groups for disbursing into a dilute aqueous solution and provide an anodic or a cathodic electrocoating composition.

As explained in U.S. Patent No. 4.241.200 (the "200 patent), an aqueous-dispersed electrocoating composition containing an aery lic-polyurethane copolymer is produced by reacting tertiary alkyl peroxide with a diisocyanate to provide a diperoxide blocked urethane prepolymer which functions as a free radical initiator in a subsequent polymerization of acrylic monomers. The polyurethane acrylic copolymer is suitable for use in either anodic or cathodic electrocoating composition.

The most useful peroxide is a t-butyl hydroxymethyl peroxide although other hydroperoxides such as t-butyl hydroperoxide and cumene hydroperoxide can be used. Tertiary-butyl hydroxymethyl peroxides can be produced by reacting molar equivalents of formaldehyde with tertiary-butyl hydro peroxide as shown by Erdy, et al., in J. of Polymer
Referring to the isocyanate compound to be reacted and capped with a tertiary alkyl peroxide, the polyisocyanate can be a di- or triisocyanate structurally illustrated as:
R-NCO

R-NCO wherein R can be the same or different and R can be either aliphatic or aromatic group. Suitable polyisocyanates are preferably diisocyanates such as 2,4 or 2,6 toluene diisocyanate, phenvlene diisocyanate, hexamethylene or tetramethylene diisocyanate, 1 ,5 -naphthalene diisocyanate, ethylene or propylene diisocyanate as well as trimethylene or triphenyl triisocyanate, and similar di- or triisocyanate. The polyisocyanate can be generally selected from the group of aliphatic, cyclo-aliphatic and aromatic polyisocyanates such as, for example, hexamethylene 1 ,6-diisocyanate; isophorone diisocyanate. 1,4-dimethyl cyclohexane. diphenylmethane diisocyanate; polymethylene polyphenyl polyisocyanate; and mixtures thereof.

The urethane diperoxide prepolymer is then copolymerized with acrylic ethylenically unsaturated monomers to provide a polyurethane-acrylic copolymer. The urethane diperoxide reacts through the peroxide linkage group wherein each peroxide becomes a free radical initiator which activates the ethylenic double bond whereby the urethane prepolymer free radical reacts with an ethylenic double bond to provide a urethane copolymer. Other activated ethylenic double bonds coreact with other monomer double bonds to provide copolymerized acrylic monomers. The urethane copolymer contains by weight at least about 10% urethane and preferably between 20% and 50% urethane with balance being copolymerized acrylic monomers with minor amounts of other ethylenically unsaturated monomers. The molecular weight of such polymers are preferably between about 3,000 and 50,000. Useful ethylenically unsaturated monomers include, for example, lower alkyl esters of acrylic or methacrylic acid such as methyl-, ethyl-propyl-, butyl-, acrylates or methacrylates, 2-methylhexyl aery late, n-octyl aery late, 2-ethylhexyl aery late, as well as similar methacrylates. Minor amounts of other ethylenic monomers include vinyl
aromatic hydrocarbons such as styrene. alpha-methyl styrene, similar alkyl styrene. vinyl toluene, vinyl naphthalene, and divinyl benzene; aliphatic hydrocarbons such as 1.3 butadiene, methyl-2-butadiene. 1 ,3-peperylene. cyclopentadiene, dicyclopentadiene, 2,3-dimethyl butadiene, and similar conjugated polyolefins; vinyl halides such as vinyl chloride and vinylidene chloride; and vinyl esters such as vinyl acetate. Particularly preferred ethylenically unsaturated monomers include alkyl acrylates and methacrylates with minor amounts of styrene, alpha-methyl styrene, t-butyl styrene, 1,3 -butadiene, isoprene, and acrylonitrile.
On a weight basis, the polyurethane-acrylic matrix copolymer contains between 10% and 90% polyurethane, between 10% and 70% acrylic monomer, and up to 50% other copolymerized ethy 1 enic monomers .

The polyurethane-acrylic polymers can be rendered water soluble by introducing pendant amine groups on the polymer to provide an aqueous electrocoating solution suitable for electrocoating onto a cathode substrate. Amine groups can be attached to the polymer by reacting free carboxyl groups with an alkyleneimine or substituted alkyleneimine as suggested in U.S. Pat. Nos. 3,679,564 and 3,617,458. The amine group is reacted with at least 1% of an acid salt proton donor to render the polymer positive ionic for electrocoating onto a cathode substrate. Useful solubilizing salts include proton donating acids such as phosphoric, sulfuric, hydrochloric, acetic, formic, lactic, and similar organic or inorganic acids.

In similar manner, polymers containing carboxyl groups can be solubilized in water by neutralizing with amine salts or bases such as KOH or NaOH and further provide an anodic electrocoating composition. Carboxyl groups can be introduced into the polymer by reacting polycarboxylic acids such as maleic, fumaric, acrylic, or methacrylic acid. Preferred carboxyhc acids are acrylic or methacrylic acid. The acid number of the polymer should be between about 20 and 200 and preferably, between 40 and 80. At least about 2% solubilizing salt such as KOH or NaOH is preferred.

The polyurethane-acrylic matrix copolymer containing hydroxyls or carboxy Is are adapted to be cross-linked with aminoplast resins such as melamine-formaldehyde. Melamine resins can be selected from melamine or melamine derivatives such as methylol melamine or similar alkylated melamine-formaldehyde reactive resins commonly referred to as aminoplast resins. Melamine resins, for instance, can cross-link hydroxyl containing polyurethane-acrylic matrix copolymers when heat cured at temperatures of about 300 °F. to 400 °F for about 20 minutes. Ordinarily about 65-70 weight parts of polyurethane-acrylic matrix copolymer mixed with about 25 to 35 weight parts melamine cross-linker provide a resin mixture containing between about 20% to 40% by weight melamine. Other cross-linkers such as blocked isocyanates, phenolic resins, etc., can also be used.

The polyurethane-acrylic matrix polymer mixed with aminoplast resin can be dispersed in water by adding polymer to a water bath containing the proper solubilizing salt such as proton donor salt for cathodic compositions and amines or bases for anodic compositions. The polymer
solids content of the electrocoating bath can be generally between 5% and 25% by weight and preferably, between 5% and 15%. The electrocoating composition can be electrocoated onto a cathode or anode substrate by passing direct electric current between the anode and cathode to electrodeposit a coating onto an anode substrate. The current is reversed for deposition onto a cathode substrate. The substrates are electrically conductive metal such as iron, steel, aluminum, galvanized steel, zinc, chromium, tin, gold, silver, copper, lead, brass, bronze, and similar electroconductive materials.

Electrocoating is carried out at a voltage above the threshold voltage of the electrocoating paint composition which is the voltage at which the polymer will electrocoat due to a direct electric current being passed through the electrocoating bath. The maximum tolerable voltage is slightly below the rupture voltage of the paint coating being applied to the substrate, where the rupture voltage is that voltage which causes the paint film already applied to rupture upon continued application of such voltage. The desirable voltage is between 20 and 500 volts and preferably between 50 and 300 volts. The temperature of the electrocoating bath is generally between 15°C and 50°C and preferably between 20°C and 35°C. Agitation is preferred to maintain uniformity of the dilute polymer solution.

The Silicon-containing Curable Synthetic Resin
The silicon-containing curable synthetic resin can be any of many silane, silicone or
20 organopolysiloxane coating compositions, such as are disclosed in U.S. Pat. Nos. 3,451,838,
4,308.317, 4,353,959, 4,615,947, and 5,120.81 1. These 13 patents are incorporated herein by reference.

I presently prefer to use a silicon-containing curable synthetic resin available from General 25 Electric Company as UVHC 8558™ silicone hard coat resin. Products of this type are disclosed in U.S. Patent Nos. 4,348,462. 5.242.719, 5,468,789. 5,607.729, and 5.712.325, which are incorporated herein by reference.

U.S. Patent No. 4,348.462 (the "462 patent) discloses a silicon-containing coating composition which does not require heat to initiate curing of the product, which is made by the -, Q combination of colloidal silica with acryloxy functional silanes or water miscible hydroxy acrylates, or preferably both, with catalytic amounts of UV-sensitive photoinitiators. The radiation curable coating composition of the '462 patent comprises: (A) 100 parts by weight of colloidal silica (SiO,). For example, Nalco 1034 is a dispersion colloidal silica of 34% and 66% water by weight, o r The dispersion of colloidal silica is used in an amount sufficient to provide 100 parts of silica by weight. Colloidal silica is available in basic or acidic form. Either may be used. However, the acidic form (low sodium content) is preferred.

To the 100 parts colloidal silica (about 294 parts by weight of the Nalco 1034 dispersion) is added (B) 5 to 500 parts, and preferably 50 to 200 parts, of an acryloxy functional silane or
glycidoxy functional silane. These silanes assist to impart high abrasion resistance to the coating compounds but it has been found that without more, adhesion is poor. To improve adhesion, there is added in addition to these acryloxy and glycidoxy functional silanes. from 10 to 500 parts, and preferably 50 to 200 parts of (C) a non-silyl acrylate material. Especially preferred acrylates are water miscible hydroxy acrylates. Non-hydroxy acrylates could be utilized but are not preferred since they are less miscible in water. In these systems water is useful as a viscosity reducing agent.

The above described ingredients are catalyzed with catalytic amounts of (D) ultraviolet light sensitive photoinitiators or blends of such initiators. Radical-type initiators can be used alone but it is preferred that a combination of radical and cationic-type photoinitiators be used for improved abrasion resistance. When acidic colloidal silica is used, it is required that there be such a combination of photoinitiators. The radical-type catalysts are used to cure the acryloxy functional portions of the composition. The cationic-type catalysts cure the siloxane portions. A combination of catalysts gives tighter cure properties and improved abrasion resistance. The catalytic amounts of these photoinitiators may vary, but ordinarily the cationic-type catalyst such as the hereinafter described onium salts are present in an amount of, approximately, 0.05 to 5.0% by weight based upon the amounts of ingredients A, B, and C. and preferably are present in an amount of from 0.1 to 1.5%. The radical type photoinitiators ordinarily are present in an amount of, approximately 0.5 to 5.0% by weight of ingredients A, B, and C, and preferably are present in an amount of, approximately. 1 to 3% by weight.

The radiation curable coating compositions are made by mixing (A) an amount of colloidal silica sufficient to provide 100 parts by weight of silica with 5 to 500 parts of (B) acryloxy or glycidoxy functional silanes or mixtures thereof, and 10 to 500 parts by weight of (C) a non-sylyl acrylate. This mixture is catalyzed by combining it with effective amounts of ultraviolet light sensitive catalysts, which preferably are a blend of radical -type and cationic-type UV catalysts.
The catalyzed compositions can then be coated by well known techniques onto selected substrates and cured by exposure to ultraviolet radiation.

However, depending upon individual desired process parameters such as rate of cure and ultimate abrasion-resistance, the amount of the photoinitiator can range from approximately 0.05 to 5 parts by weight per 100 parts of the mixture of ingredient A, B. and C.

These cationic photoinitiators are particularly effective for initiating a cross-linking reaction upon exposure to ultraviolet radiation. Good hard coatings having excellent adhesion can thus be obtained when the coating composition is applied to a substrate and exposed to radiation such as that provided by UV lamps.

Improved abrasion-resistance is obtained with the same hard coating compositions when in addition to the cationic photoinitiators described above, there is also utilized a radical-type initiator which is effective for cross-linking or self-condensing the acryloxy-functional portions of the silanes contained in the composition. 20 for at least 10 seconds at a temperature between about 100°F andabout200°F. The acid wash can be any suitable commercially available material. As indicated above, my presently preferred process for electrodeposition of polyurethane on metal surfaces is disclosed in ClearClad Coatings, Inc.'s Installation and Operation Manual (Appendix 1) (Release Number 2.0, Manual Serial Number: 1 192, copyrighted 1997 by

ClearClad Coatings, Inc.). The electrodeposition process described in the Manual is referred to as electrophoretic coating. The process deposits a cross-linked organic polyurethane lacquer coating to any metal with proper treatment as described in the Manual. The coating can be clear or colored with pigment, translucent or opaque, and has uniform thickness over the coated surface, usually in the range of 1 - 100 microns (.00004"-.0040").

For coating aluminum and magnesium surfaces, I prefer to use ClearClad LCX® polyurethane/acrylic electrocoat enamel supplied by ClearClad Coatings, Inc., and which is described in the Manual on page 48. The ClearClad urethane/acrylic coating material is supplied as a concentrate, which is diluted with deionized water to form an emulsion coating bath in a coating tank 34 (FIG. 2). Electrodes (anodes), not shown, are placed in the coating bath and made anodic (+) in a direct current (DC) circuit (not shown). The work piece to be coated is placed in the bath and made cathodic (-). As current flows, the resinous polyurethane/acrylic material in the emulsion deposits on the substrate work piece 10. The deposited polyurethane/acrylic is an insulator, and as it coats the metallic substrate, current flow is reduced until the electrodeposition stops. Thus, the coating process gives a uniform thickness over the substrate. Typical time required to apply the polyurethane/acrylic base coat 12 is 30-200 seconds. The final coating thickness is proportional to the voltage applied to the DC source, which generally is in the 10-150 volt range. The higher the voltage, the longer the electrodeposition. and therefore the thicker the deposited polyurethane/acrylic film required to insulate the substrate and stop the coating process.

The electrodeposition process continues until all conductive areas on the workpiece are insulated, giving a uniform thickness over the part being coated. The self-limiting characteristic of the coating process results in good "throwing power" into hard-to coat places. To start
coating, the voltage is slowly "ramped up" either automatically or manually to the desired final voltage, which remains on for the time required to achieve a complete and uniform coat. Simple surfaces are completely coated in a relatively short time. Surfaces with complex configurations require longer coating time, which is easily determined by simple experimentation. I prefer to deposit a polyurethane/acrylic film which results in a final cured base coat with a thickness between about 2 and about 100 microns (.00004"-.0040"). The base coat can either be clear, or contain pigment, as described in the prior art cited above.

After the substrate is coated with the base coat, it is removed from the coating tank 34 and passed through a tenth rinse stage 36 to remove excess coating material as described in the ClearClad Manual on pages 1-10.

After the excess coating material is removed by rinsing in the tenth rinse stage 36. the work piece is passed through an eleventh rinse stage 38 in deionized water. Thereafter, the polyurethane/acrylic base coat is air dried at drying stage 40 for three to ten or more minutes, depending upon the complexity of the work piece, to allow water to evaporate. The base coat is then subjected to a curing stage 42 in an air-circulated oven (not shown) free of airborne particulate matter, and capable of maintaining the work piece at the desired temperature for up to 15 minutes. Usually, a complete cure is achieved in about 5 minutes, especially if the air-circulated oven uses heated air supplemented by infrared radiation. Ordinarily, the cure takes place at a temperature between about 200°F to about 375°F. The actual curing temperature depends on the particular coating composition used, and is easily determined by simple experimentation.

An Overview of Electrophoretic Coating
Electrophoretic Coating, sometimes referred to as E-Coat, is a general term describing the application of organic coatings (Lacquers) to metallic substrates through the use of electric currents.

As one might imagine, there are a vast number of formulations and techniques within the whole field of electrophoretic coatings. Additionally, these coatings can be can be further categorized into two groups which make the item to be coated either anodic (+) or cathodic (-) in a direct current circuit. For our purposes here we will discuss primarily ClearClad cathodic coatings which employ state of the art techniques developed over many years of experience endeavoring to maximize the quality and properties of these films as well as ease of application.

The ClearClad process deposits a cross linked organic polyurethane lacquer coating to any metal with proper pretreatment. The coating can be clear or colored, translucent or opaque, and has uniform thickness over the pan, typically in the 10-20 microns (.0004" - .0008") range. It is extremely durable resisting the affects of chemicals, tarnishing, abrasion and ultraviolet light.

ClearClad is applied using, what is termed, an electrophoretic deposition process. This is a method to uniformly deposit the resinous material which makes up the lacquer coating before curing through electrodeposition techniques.
The equipment to accomplish the coating looks remarkably like electroplating equipment but that is where any analogy stops in many ways, especially as regards environmental impact.

The electrodeposition process for ClearClad can be described in a general way as fellows. ClearClad is supplied as a concentrate which is diluted with deionized water to form an emulsion in the coating tank that is stable over a specific pH range in the mild acid regioa Electrodes (anodes) are placed in the coating bath and made anodic (+) on a direct current (DC) power source. ' The article(s) to be coated are placed in the bath and made cathodic (-) on the same power source. As current flows electrolysis of the water takes place, oxygen and hydrogen are evolved at the respective electrodes, the anodes and the work, and, at the work to be coated (cathode), a thin layer of alkalinity forms at the interface with the solution. The resinous material in the solution becomes unstable at this alkaline interface and coagulates on the work.

The resins, as deposited on the work, are an electrical insulator and as the coating adheres on the work the current is reduced until the electrolysis stops and deposition of resinous material is terminated. The coating process continues until all conductive areas on the work are insulated giving a uniform thickness over the part being coated and good "throwing power" into generally hard to coat places. Typical time required to apply the coat is 45-90 seconds.

With this system, the coating thickness is proportional to the voltage applied from the DC source, generally in the 25-75 volt range. This is, for example, because a higher voltage can sustain 5 electrolysis longer and needs a heavier film to insulate the substrate and limit electrolysis and stop the coating process and vice versa.

One can quickly see the why electrophoretic coating is not really analogous to electroplating. An electroplated layer of metal depends on the current (ionic conduction) through the solution where metal ions in the plating solution are reduced at the work (cathode) in the form of metal. The thickness of the plated metal layer at any point on the surface depends on the amount of current at that point and i o the length of time that it was exposed to this current flow. As a result plating tends to be non uniform in thickness since it is virtually impossible to maintain uniform current over the entire surface of a part.

The differences between electroplating, that requires ionic conduction, and electrophoretic coating that requires it only to sustain a small amount of electrolysis of the water portion of the coating bath, bring out an important point that will be stressed throughout this manual. That is, cleanliness of the coating bath and the necessary steps, on a production basis, to maintain the required level of cleanliness.

The best indicator of the cleanliness of the coating bath is it's electrical conductivity. If an electrophoretic coating bath becomes too conductive, leading to increased ionic conduction, there is more gas evolved at the electrodes. At the work, excessive gassing will cause major problems in the coagulated resinous material as deposited. The importance of bath cleanliness and proper control cannot be emphasized enough.

On exiting the coating tank, the electrodeposited film of ClearClad need be only rinsed, air dried if one ^υ chooses and oven cured after the coating operatioa Information on these subsequent steps will be covered in more detail later in this manual.

The ultra filtration unit (UF) is a means by which water and water soluble materials may be removed from the ClearClad bath while retaining the ClearClad resins and returning them to the coating bath. The -key items that take place are: a) The solids content of the coating bath is reduced as the coating is formed on the work and the acid content of the bath is increased. b) Despite all precautions to avoid it, some contamination may be dragged in to the coating bath that will contaminate the coating bath, since it is an electrolyte, raising it's conductivity. c) Solid materials from the coating bath will be dragged out on the coated work and will be rinsed off in the subsequent rinse. In the recommended closed loop installation shown in figure 2, the UF unit provides a unique capability to control these changes that are happening to the bath during coating. The UF unit, put simply, is a membrane filter that allows the large particles (resin solids) to be concentrated and returned to the coating tank while the small particles, water, electrolytes, acids and some solvent are "Permeated" through the membrane and returned to the closed drag out tank.

The portion of this permeate stream returning to the drag out tank is passed through an Ion Trap (IT) to remove ionic contamination that would increase the conductivity of the coating tank.

Mixing of ClearClad Concentrates/ Additives and New Bath Make Up

ClearClad products are provided primarily as concentrates that must be diluted with a diluent, either de-ionized water or existing bath material (de-ionized water if making a new bath, bath material if making replenishments to an existing bath). In this section we will discuss the proper methods for dilution of ClearClad concentrates (often referred to as "letting down" the ClearClad concentrate) and addition of color agents, matting agents, solvents, etc. Due to the diversity of ClearClad product types and additives, a system of off-line pre-mixing is recommended for facilitating both new bath make-up and production bath replenishment. As the physical and chemical nature of different ClearClad products can vary greatly, the effectiveness of the mixing and diluting of these is important to the ultimate quality of the process and the final product. Certain products may be added directly to the bath without pre-mixing and this capability will be stated on the appropriate data sheet. However, it should be assumed that all products need pre-mixing unless otherwise stated.

Off-line premixing involves the "charging" of paint concentrate into a suitable pre-mixing tank where mixing with additives (where appropriate) and D.I.water/bath material for pre-dilution is accomplished using mechanical stirring (see figure 4). When pre-dilution is complete, all or some of the charge is transferred directly into the process bath via the weir so that final incorporation is accomplished via the bath circulation system (In the case of a new bath make up the pre-diluted material would be introduced through a filter directly into the coating tank until the system was completely filled and circulation could be started).

The pre-mixing tank and stirrer combination may range from a laboratory beaker & spatula for very small installations to specifically designed and built stainless steel tanks with permanent motorized mixers for larger operations. However, in all sizes of operation, a propeller-type motorized mixer is recommended as this will give the best emulsification through effective mixing. Any mixer should have sufficient torque to create a vortex at all stages of mixing and dilution. Electric-motor driven mixers are the most versatile. Suitable types range from small laboratory models

(0.5 - 10 liters mixing capability) to industrial grades with several hundred liter mixing capability. Small installation pre-mixing may utilize cordless electric drills with a suitable propeller attachment - the more powerful 9.6v types are recommended capable of 1500 r.p.m. with higher torque. Air-motor driven mixers are available especially in medium to large industrial sizes.
Important Note: In the case of medium to large scale mixes, if ambient temperatures in the mixing environment are around 90 "F or higher, then attention must be paid to the flash point of the

ClearClad materials. In these circumstances, air-motor driven mixers are ideal. Fixed electric motors should be of the explosion proof type. In the case of small scale mixes using cordless drills or removable electric motors, there is a pre-blending method given below to cope with this situation.

For the stirrer, stainless steel is the typically used material.

Ultrafiltration Design and Operation Considerations
In order to understand the need for and advantages of ultrafiltration, the following processes which occur during the ClearClad coating operation should be reviewed.
1 ) As the solids content is reduced in the bath by formation of the coating on the work, the acid content of the coating bath is increased.
2) Ionic Contamination of the coating bath, an electrolyte, will most probably take place due to "carrying in" of contaminates from processes up stream.
3) Drag out of coating resinous solids material will take place as racks of work leave the coating tank and will end up in the first rinse after the coating tank.

Items 1) and 2) above will have a direct influence on the coating quality and the stability of the coating bath. Item 3), if there is no subsequent recovery of materials dragged out of the coating bath, will result in poor utilization of the coating material and environmental problems due to a significant solids content in the effluent going to the drain.

A properly installed and utilized closed loop ultrafiltration process will allow good control over the acid content of the coating bath and enable nearly 100% usage of the coating bath materials without creation of effluent solids that must be dealt with for proper pollution control.

Figure 5 shows how a typical ultrafilter membrane functions. The stream from the coating tank weir (see figure 2) contains not only large resin particles of resin solids but small particles, water,

This latter group is "permeated" through the membrane while the large particles, the resin solids, are concentrated and returned to the coating tank.

The unique ability of the ultrafilter membrane to separate the resinous solid materials from the other materials, some of which are contaminants, yields an ability to assemble and operate a most efficient coating system. To gain a better understanding of the reasons for this we should review the possible systems that could be assembled with a UF unit. The key point in each of the systems is how the o permeate is utilized, there are three possible ways.

1) Simple bath purification ("Kidney unit") - Operating in this mode, unlike the system shown in figure 2, most or all of the permeate produced is dumped to waste in order to eliminate water soluble contaminants.

This system has major disadvantages in that: 5 a) There is a continual significant volume loss from the coating system, equivalent to the amount of permeate dumped, which has to be made up with deionized water. b) The non-contaminant constituents of the permeate (solvents, emulsion stabilizer, etc.) will be depleted from the coating bath faster than they can be replaced by the normal introduction of replenishing feed. This will necessitate overly frequent bath analysis in order to monitor losses, and make the required additions of replenishers. 0

2) Closed-loop reclaim - In this mode, a minor portion of the permeate is dumped to effect purification, but the majority is recycled back to the coating bath via the drag out tank. This drag out tank, which is being continually fed with permeate, rinses off the dragged out bath material from the coated components and, being counter flowed back into the coating bath, facilitates reclamation of the dragged out solids. Permeate sprays can be used over either or both the coating and drag out tanks in order to improve rinsing. 5

Advantages: a) Almost 100% utilization of coating material is possible. b) Permeate is a very effective rinsing medium. 0 Disadvantages: a) Greater permeate production is required than the "Kidney unit" system in order to provide sufficient volumes for both purification and reclamation.

5
b) Recycling of a major portion of the contaminants is unavoidable due to the "closed loop" nature of this mode of operation. c) There is still some volume change in the system due to the quantity of permeate dumped.

3) TRAP System - This concept - Total Reclaim And Purification - addresses the problems of the two previous systems by the introduction of ion exchange technology into the "closed loop". This is the recommended mode of operation and is the one diagramed in figure 2 of this manual. The Ion Trap introduced in the permeate return path to the drag out tank 0 provides ion exchange resins which selectively remove contaminants from the permeate, leaving the non-contaminating bath constituents present.

Advantages: a) Only minimal quantities of permeate need be dumped. 5 b) There is minimal volume loss from the system. c) There is minimal, and easily controllable, loss of solvents, stabilizers, etc. from the system. d) Recycling of harmful contaminants through the closed loop system is avoided.

In this mode of operation, with only a small percentage of permeate waste, TRAP enables the o purification effect of 100% permeate dumping, as in system 1) above, by selective contaminant removal. Accordingly, the greatest proportion of permeate can be utilized for rinsing and reclaiming.

With the TRAP system, the amount of permeate dumping required will vary with the particular coating application. In order to control VOC, there may be a minimum volume of dumped permeate per unit of replenisher concentrate added. This is normally sufficient to account for any traces of contaminants "missed" by the TRAP. However, in applications where 5 contamination rates are unusually high, special attention may be required.

In certain applications, using this "closed loop" concept in operations requiring large amounts of permeate to be discarded, where possible, some permeate should be returned to the drag out tank. This can prevent a dangerous situation caused by excessive depletion of acid in the bath. If this occurs, the

This can result in large decreases in conductivity and the process becomes difficult to operate. Also, if the MEQ is allowed to go too high, the converse can occur. The ClearClad emulsion can become so densely packed that ultrafiltration becomes difficult making further acid removal difficult.

Proper use of ultrafiltration allows a means where the acid and any contaminants may be removed from the coating system independently of the solids. It is recommended that ultrafiltration systems for ClearClad installations be operated on a continuous basis (24 hours/day). TRAP System Design Criteria General

The key to running a productive and efficient E-Coating system lies in the use of an ultrafiltration system based on the TRAP principle described on page 24, earlier in this manual. Although operation with other systems described in this same section of this manual is possible, we strongly recommend use of a TRAP system for the reasons discussed earlier. What we will do in this section will be to discuss the criteria for design and implementation of a TRAP System. This design is based on the adherence to certain basic rules for this system. They are: a) The basic coating system should consist of two tanks of approximately the same size and configuration (see figure 2 of this manual under Equipment Required and Preparation). Each tank should have a weir which is approximately 10% of it's volume. b) The output of solids from the U F tube, returned to the coating tank, must provide for an certain number of turnovers of the coating tank per hour: i.e. the number of times the coating tank volume is completely changed each hour. The turnover rates that should be observed depends on the type of bath you are installing. For clear baths the rate should be in the 3-5 turnovers per hour while pigmented or baths with matting agents should have turnovers in the 8-10 range. c) The output of permeate from the U/F tube should be approximately 10% of the drag out tank volume per hour (this assumes that the coating tank and drag out tanks are of similar volume).

In other words, this permeate output, piped to the drag out tank, should completely change the drag out approximately 10 hours. Since the drag out tank is cross feed into the coating tank, the coating tank will also receive an input of permeate equivalent to it's volume every 10 hours which is our objective.

Given these basic design rules, we will take on a specific system design to use as an example. For our example, we will assume that we are designing a coating tank that will be 100 gallons (approx. 380 liters) and that we will be running a clear ClearClad coating bath without any pigments or matting agents. We will have a drag out tank of the same approximate volume. Both tanks will have weirs of approximately 10 gallons (38 liters).

Of the rules b) and c) above, the overriding one in designing this system is c) which calls for a specific amount permeate production to turnover the drag out tank approximately every ten hours. The turnover of the coating tank is nonetheless important, however, that is easily accomplished and will be explained in more detail later. Other TRAP System Design and Start Up Considerations

Automatic De-ionized Water Additions - A very important point that must be dealt with is protection against the possibility of the U/F system running dry. As recommended, these systems should be run , , continuously, 7 days/week, 24 hours/day and therefore are often running unattended. If the bath is maintained and used daily, generally there is no problem since operators will be making adds, removing permeate and adding make-up deionized water. However, experience has shown that at some installations, after runs are completed the system may not be used for a period of time and it can be, literally, ignored.

Without routine maintenance, difficult but avoidable problems may take place. The TRAP system will continue to circulate, there will be solution losses due to evaporation and other causes. Should the 0 solution level in the drag out tank fall too low, overflow into the drag out tank weir will stop. Soon the level in the coating tank will fall also because of no cross feed from the drag out tank and it will stop overflowing into it's weir also. At this point the coating tank weir will run dry. The U/F pump will begin to suck air and inject that air into the system. This will cause severe damage to the solution itself and the U/F membrane tube as well.

A simple solution for this problem should be put in place at installation. You will note in the system 25 diagram (Figure 2) that a solenoid valve is shown controlling the feed of deionized water into the drag out tank. Turning the solenoid valve on and off to replenish the level in the drag out tank is easily accomplished through the use of a micro-float switch in the drag out tank adjusted to the control level desired. This precaution is highly recommended!

Plumbing Considerations - As pointed out in Section 3 of this manual, wherever possible hard piping of schedule 80 PVC or equivalent should be used. Additionally, in the piping of the TRAP system, care 3 should be taken to minimize pressure drops in the piping of the system. What is meant by minimizing pressure drop is basically to avoid sharp bends and elbows wherever possible (use of the newer "sweep" bends is recommended). Also, use piping large enough for the flows that will be encountered (in our example tank, for the 17 GPM flow needed, 1 " i.d. PVC should be used).

35
Important Note: You will note in the system diagram (figure #2) that there is a valve (F) installed between the output of the primary pump supplying solution to the U/F unit and the input to the U/F unit. The purpose of this valve is as follows. At system start up the valve should be closed and gradually opened as the system starts to avoid "shocking" the U/F unit with a sudden application of pressure. This could damage the U/F membranes. Additionally, it should be closed when shutting down the system to avoid complete drainage of the U/F membrane during the shut down period. Complete drainage could cause drying out of the membrane and possible clogging.

Also, in setting up the system, either the drag out tank itself or just the drag out tank weir needs to be marginally higher than the coating tank. Something like 1/2"- 1 " higher is adequate. The purpose is to always have a positive pressure from the drag out tank to the coating tank so that solution will flow from the" drag out tank to the coating tank through the cross feed connection.

In the attachment of the cross feed connection to the drag out tank weir it is a good idea, on the inside of the tank weir wall, to put a 90° elbow turned up vertically. A pipe nipple of suitable length can be attached to this elbow and serve as a method to adjust the drag out tank weir height. Also, this will preclude any significant back flow from the coating tank should the level in the drag out tank drop for any reason.

Cleaning of New U/F Membranes Tubes - When setting up a new system U/F membrane tube (or replacing an existing one) we recommend the following cleaning procedure before installing it in the system. Generally, these membrane tubes are shipped with a glycerin type preservative on the membrane fibers. In a suitable container having a volume of at least 6-10 times the volume of the membrane mbe make up the following solution. a) Fill the container 3/4 full with de-ionized water. b) Add Emulsion Stabilizer (440A324)" to bring the pH down to approximately 4.0 c) To this volume of solution add approximately 5-10% (by volume) of Solvent replenisher (430A264)
This assumes you are cleaning the membrane tube for use on a cathodic system, were you going to use it on an anodic system Anodic DIPA Solution (440A057) would be used.

If a pump is available, connect it from this reservoir of solution to the U/F membrane and back into the reservoir (it may be necessary to cap the permeate output port). Circulate this solution through the U/F membrane for about 10 minutes. Should a pump not be available to circulate the solution it may be done manually but care must be taken to see that the circulation is vigorous enough through the U/F unit, it should be at a rate of at least 10 GPM. When this is accomplished, the unit is ready for installation into the TRAP system.

Testing Before Start up - With the TRAP system piped and completely installed to the tanks to be used, a "wet test" using only deionized water and approximately 2% Solvent Replenisher (430A264) is appropriate (Do not use straight de-ionized water, some membranes can be damaged if de-ionized water only is used). Certainly, you want to check for leaks and general system integrity, however, you also want to see what kind of flow you are getting in the coating tank. Once the ClearClad solution is installed ascertaining flow is difficult due to the opaque nature of the ClearClad solution.

You want to be sure that there is uniform flow of solution over the parts to be coated when they are in the coating tank. If the flow is too fast it can "wash" the solution away before it has a chance to adhere to the item being coated. Should it be too slow, there may not be enough solution available to coat the item properly.

By fashioning a simple flag on the end of a stick and moving it about in the coating tank when it is circulating just water you can easily see the action in the tank and watch for "dead" spots or areas of high flow or turbulence. Should these be encountered, adjustment of the sparger tube in the coating tank would be the first course of action.

Filtration - As shown on the system diagram, two types of filtering devices can be used. One, marked "S" on the diagram is intended to be a coarse filter in front of the input to the U F mbe. This is very important to protect the U/F tube and must not be omitted. Also shown is a secondary filtering loop, marked "F" in the diagram, drawing from and returning to the coating tank. The purpose of this filter loop is to remove any fine paniculate through the use of a fine size filter cartridge, typically in the 5-10 micron range. It should be pointed out that we are aware that these two filtering devices could be consolidated into one filter, the one marked "S" in the diagram. In some installations, instead of using a strainer or coarse filter users have made use of filter bags, typically 5 microns, which will filter out both fine paniculate as well as gross particles. However, we do not recommend doing this. We recommend using separate a paniculate filter and separate strainer. The reason for this is that should foreign particles get into the coating bath that are too heavy to be' sent up and over the tank weir, they will never be removed from the bath. An example could be rust panicles. Having the separate paniculate filter loop insures their removal.

The use of direct heaters like electrical immersion heaters, although convenient, is not generally recommended except for very small baths (50 gallons or less). Even in that case we do not recommend use of metal sheath heaters, but would advise only use of quartz heaters having an internal element with a quartz outer sheath and a protective guard of teflon. When using direct heaters of this kind extreme care must be taken to insure uniform flow in the tank and around the heater to guard against hot spots and temperature stratification in the coating tank.'

Colored ClearClad Coatings
ClearClad coatings may be modified with dyes or pigments to give attractive finishes over many metals. Two type of colored finishes can be achieved. Tney are:
1) "Opaque" or "hard" - A coating of this type is where the substrate is not visible, all light is reflected from the surface of the coating itself.
2) "Transparent" - This is where the substrate is visible, but modified in color and appearance by the coating.
The opaque or hard coating, 1) above, is essentially a paint and effectively opaque. The transparent coating, 2) above, is more complicated and requires additional explanation.

To achieve any particular effect with transparent coatings of various colors, it is necessary to understand the mechanism of color filtration and reflection. Any light reflective surface has three main attributes. They are: a) Luminosity - That is, how much light is reflected. b) Color - That is, the spectral response of the light reflected. c) Gloss - That is, the specular coherence of the light reflected.
In the cases of most metals encountered for coating, the substrates generally have medium to high luminosity, they are white or yellow in color and often have high gloss. The transparent colored
ClearClad coatings will become a filter over such substrates and modify the color. This modification will only take place within the following limits..

First, the luminosity of the substrates cannot be increased. For example, it is not really possible to modify the conventional bright nickel to exactly simulate gold and brass. This is because the bright nickel is intrinsically darker (that is, it has lower luminosity than both gold and brass).

Second, color absorbed by the substrate cannot be added. For example, it is nearly impossible to make a brass appear blue by coating it with a blue transparent ClearClad. This is because, the base brass metal already absorbs the blue component of white light thereby giving the characteristic brass color.

Succinctly, the effect gained by use of transparent colors over base metals depends heavily on the luminosity, color and gloss of the base metal. A typical gold colored transparent ClearClad bath applied over bright silver plate yields a color that is close to Swiss gold color standard 2N 18 (i.e. 18 kt gold). The same bath applied to bright nickel plated parts yields a gold color but towards a very greenish gold. When applied directly to zinc die cast parts the color, although unique, becomes a very green color with
only a slight tinge of gold.

An endless variety of colors, transparent or opaque are possible with ClearClad coatings. Your ClearClad distributor can provide you with formulas for many colors. For special opaque colors, if you provide ClearClad Coatings, Inc., through your distributor, a color sample of the color desired, almost any color can be matched.

If you are looking for a special effect with a transparent color you should provide a sample of the substrate you wish to coat as well a final color sample so that a proper determination of feasibility for that color on that particular substrate can be made.

Coverage of ClearClad Coatings

The coverage of ClearClad materials is directly proportional to the amount of resinous solid materials present in the bath and may be calculated on the basis of the amount of solid that each liter of concentrate adds to the bath.

As with any coating, the thinner it is deposited, the more area it will cover. The coverage can be calculated by figuring the volume of coating that the coated area will have on it. For example, if we were to coat a part having one square foot of area (144 in2* or 929 cm2) with a thickness of 10 microns (0.001 cm) the volume of coating would be 0.929 cm3.

Each liter of ClearClad concentrate contains approximately 50% solids, the resinous material that will make up the coating, at an approximate specific gravity of 1.1 grams (gm) per cubic centimeter (cm3) (for clear and translucent colors). Therefore, in one liter of ClearClad concentrate there are 500 cm3 (50% of 1 liter) divided by 1.1 gm/cm3 or 454 cm3 of solids available to form the coating. Since we needed 0.929 cm3 of coating (1 foot square at 10 microns thickness) for the coating in our example, we will use 0.929 divided by 454 or .00205 liters of concentrate. Alternately, we can see that one liter of ClearClad concentrate will cover 454 divided by 1.1 or 489 ft2 per liter.

Some other coatings, such as opaque colors, cover less area since the specific gravity is higher due to the required pigments for coloring. For example, a liter of white (the worst case) has a specific gravity of approximately 1.6 gm/cm3 so it's coverage, at 10 microns, is reduced to about 336 ft2.

This is a most diverse subject. The variety of base metals and base metal conditions that are often required to coat can provide an almost endless range of possibilities for the pretreatment. Miscellaneous Tests Curing

A good test for proper curing is through the use of an Acetone Rub Test. It is performed as follows: a) Take a cotton ball, similar to those available for medical and first aid purposes, and saturate it with acetone. b) On the coated part to be tested for curing, rub an area by pushing forward with moderate

10 pressure about 1 " (2.5 cm). Pull back the same distance. This constitutes one double-rub. Each double rub should take about one second. c) Continue rubbing until the signs of break through of the coating to base metal are noticed keeping track of the number of double-rubs.

As a practical matter, properly cured ClearClad coatings will stand many hundreds of rubs, some even in excess of 1000 doubie-rubs. However, if the coating is not properly cured, break through will occur 15 at a relatively small number of double-rubs, perhaps in the area of 10-50 double-rubs.
Adhesion

Adhesion of the deposited and cured coating is very' important and needs to be checked periodically. Generally speaking, poor adhesion is a function of the pre-cleaning and preparation of the base metal 20 before entering the coating bath. A quick test to prove adhesion after curing is outlined below. It is a good idea to take frequent samples throughout a production mns to insure good adhesion is maintained. This is sometimes referred to as a "Crosshatch Adhesion test".
1 ) Allow the coated part to return to room temperature after curing.

2) Using a straight edge and a sharp blade instrument like a single edge razor blade or an ^ "Exacto" knife cut some lines through the coating down the base metal on the item being tested about 3/8"-l/2" long. Make a series of cuts (about 8-10), all in the same direction, and about .040" (1 mm) apart. For reference, 1/16" is approximately .060" and 1/32" is approximately .030".

3) Turn the straight edge 90°, perpendicular to the lines created in 2) above and make a similar cuts so that there is created a series of small squares in this pattern approximately .040" (I mm) square.
4) Apply a piece of transparent tape, pressing down hard to insure adhesion, to the "Crosshatch"

35
area created leaving a length of tape as a tab. Pull up quickly on the tape tab removing the tape from the Crosshatch area. Examine the tape and the Crosshatch area to see if any of the small squares have lifted from the base metal. If none have lifted, re-tape and do this test several times.
An indication of good adhesion is if no "squares" lift from the substrate. If some do lift, the number may give a relative indication of the adhesion but good adhesion dictates that none should lift.
Other Product, Process and Operation Tips
Corrosion Resistance

Often, especially for exterior parts that will be exposed to "weather" it is required to improve the corrosion resistance of the coated metal part. With proper design of the coating system the "salt spray" or "weatherability" of the coated metal parts can be improved dramatically.

One way to accomplish this is to use the "Interpas" version of the appropriate ClearClad product being used. These are ClearClad products HDX-I and LCB-I. In some applications, such as brass, there is a down side to their use in that there is a slight darkening of the coated part.

An alternative method is to use an electrolytic chromate step which is introduced after the acid dip before the ClearClad bath. In the case of the Plumber's brass sequence described under the Typical Pretreatments section preceding, the acid dip may be replaced by the chromate step. Very thorough rinsing must be done after this chromate step before entering the ClearClad bath! Chromate coatings are also available for zinc base metals as well.

15 Additionally, the use of phosphate coatings on steel base metals before coating will significantly improve the corrosion resistance of the finished part. They can be of either the zinc or iron type phosphate coatings. ClearClad Coatings, Inc. can provide information on recommended chromate conversion coatings or phosphating coatings for your particular applications.

INTRODUCTION

*5 The phosphoric acid/nitric acid chemical polishing bath (bright dip) is widely used to produce specular finishes on a variety of aluminum alloys used for automotive, appliance and architectural trim. Consistent production of a high quality finish requires a thorough understanding of the bright dip bath and its function, as well as careful control of the entire finishing process. This process manual addresses all phases of the bright aluminum finishing process, including pretreatments as well as the anodizing and sealing steps required to protect the bright finish.

Mechanical finishing may be used to provide a variety of surface textures on aluminum. For bright , trim, buffing is required to remove surface scratches, rolling marks and die lines, thus providing a surface which is free of surface defects. A properly designed and operated cleaning cycle is required to remove all lubricants, buffing compounds and surface oxides which would interfere with the brightening process. The bright dip bath functions by leveling the microscopic roughness of the aluminum surface, thus reducing the amount of light which is scattered and increasing the specularity of the surface. After bright dipping, most finishers utilize a sulfuric acid anodizing process to produce a clear, protective oxide coating on the metal surface. That oxide coating is then partially converted to an insoluble, hydrated alumina which closes the coating's microscopic j 5 pores and protects it from corrosion. Bright Dipping Aluminum discusses the function of each of these process steps, and outlines the control requirements for each.

MECHANICAL FINISHING

M echaπical finishing refers to operations which aiterthe surface and appearance of an aluminum part by physical means such as grinding, polishing, buffing, shot blasting or tumbling. The main objectives of these processes are to ( 1 ) remove metal surface irregularities and imperfections in order to smooth the metal surtace or (2) apply a texture to the surface of the part The method and extent to which mechanical finishing is used will depend upon the initial state of the metal surface, the method of manufacture of the article and the finish desired.
There are five types of wheel grinding and polishing operations commonly used on aluminum:
1 ) Texture or Scratch Brushing
2) Grinding 3 Roughing 0 4) Polishing
5) Buffing
Although all of these operations are used by bright anodizers to some extent, buffing is the most freαuently used type of mechanical finishing.

BUFFING 5 Buffing is used to remove minor scratches and die lines and to increase the specularity of the aluminum part. It is as much an art as a science since the skill and experience of the operator play a significant role in the final results. The buffer must strike a balance between the quality and the cost of the finish by tailoring buffing sequences and materials to the alloy, shape, and surface condition of the part. Although prior experience is invaluable in tailoring the process conditions to the part, following a few basic guidelines can minimize buffing problems and rejection due to improper buffing. 0 Finishing begins the moment raw material is received in the plant. Material handling, storage, tools and press practice all may effect both the buffing operation and the final appearance of the part. Further, the best of buffing procedures and techniques can be completely negated by careless handling after buffing. Freshly buffed surfaces should be protected against fingerprint corrosion by wiping them with a whiting compound such as calcium carbonate. In addition, buffed parts should be carefully racked on suitable trays to prevent traffic damage.
OPTIMIZING CONDITIONS 5

In the mechanical finishing of aluminum it is best to use only buffing operations and to avoid polishing whenever possible. The coarse abrasives of the polishing belts cause scratch patterns which are extremely difficult to remove with subsequent buffing. This becomes even more significant in the finishing of long sections where all work is unidirectional.

If uniform chemical treatment is to be accomplished, all preexisting oxide must be removed and removed uniformly. A common error is to under-buff. Many times the parts appear visually "clean'' -, or bright after buffing yet show defects after bright dipping. Tests have shown superior coloring results when a caustic treatment is added between cutting and coloring. Although this sequence may not be economical, it does point out the need for adequate oxide removal.
Pressure
The contact pressure of the buff on the work piece is as important as the selection of compound and buff material, and must be determined empirically for each part. Excessive contact pressure

35 will distort the buff and cause uneven wear and an infeπor surt ice finish. Furthermore, buffs under excessive pressure do not retain the compound which does Me cutting or coloring. The wheel is simply a soft cloth acting as a carrier for the compouπα, and cutting action does not come from the contact of the cloth on the metal
High contact pressures are also a cause of rapid heat buildup on the work. Temperatures beyond , 400°F / 204βC can cause metallurgical changes in the aluminum and can cause cloudiness of the anodic coating in the areas where overheating occurred. Other factors which eflect temperature are the buff material, degree of ventilation and thread count of cloth.
Compound Application

The application of compound to the buff is a critical operation. Beyond the optimum amount, additional compound will not increase metal removal. Excess compound results in the buildup of 10 residues on the parts which are often difficult to remove. As a rule excessive compound is applied when compound is applied infrequently; the wheel then has either too much or too little material at any given time. At low compound levels there is little metal removal. At high compound levels too much compound is deposited on the work. Ideally, the compound should be applied frequently in small amounts to minimize deviation from the optimum.
Speed
15 A peripheral wheel speed of 7000 ft min. has been found most desirable for buffing aluminum. This is an average speed and some adjustment based on part configuration and size is necessary.

The direction of part travel in relation to buff rotation has an effect on surface condition. Considerably more cutting occurs when the part is passed opposing or "against" wheel rotation than when the part is passed complementing or with wheel rotation. Preferably cutting and coloring should be done in the same direction and with the rotation of the wheel to prevent skip and drag. 2o For best results, cutting and coloring should be accomplished using different compounds and wheels.
Alloy

Metal selection has an effect on the surface obtained after buffing and bright anodizing. Harder metals with finer grain size give best results. In addition, they tend to be more "ding" resistant during subsequent handling. For best results, the hardest material temper compatible with required 25 formability should be utilized in fabricating the part.
Buffing Compounds

An abrasive material is the significant ingredient of either solid or liquid buffing compounds. A bar of buffing compound is a cutting material (abrasive) held together by bonding agents such as greases, stearic acid, and waxes. The abrasive material may also be formulated as a water -.n emulsion of oils to make the composite sprayable. Automatic multiple station buffing operations will normally use liquid compounds. Bar compound use is restricted to hand operations. For a compound to be effective it must be tenacious enough to adhere to the wheel, but this is the same property which makes a part difficult to clean prior to bright anodizing. By working with suppliers and on-the-job testing, the proper binder can be chosen.

The abrasive most commonly used is tripoli, a naturally occurring material composed primarily of amorphous silica with up to 5 percent iron oxide. Iron oxide is responsible for the reddish color, 35 and increasing amounts of iron oxide deepen the color. Tripoli is the most widely used buffing compound for aluminum finishing because of its availability and low cost. However, there is the potential hazard of iron oxide retention on the surface of the buffed piece. The iron oxide is not apparent after buffing, and is probably chemically bonded to the surface. If not removed with a mild-etching cleaner, the particles may cause dull or lightly pitted areas during bright dipping.

White amorphous silica, an iron-free abrasive, is occasionally used for color buffing aluminum. This substance is quite soft, however, and accomplishes little cutting.
A third abrasive, aluminum oxide (AljO,), is very hard and has good cutting and coloring properties. Formulations containing this abrasive are more costly than the others. However, where metal removal and surface contamination are critical, it may be less expensive in the long run. In a multiple station buffing sequence (cut and color), alumina should be used for the coloring stations. Buffs
A great many buff types are available and they, too, should be tailored to the job. Again, vendors' recommendations and shop testing determine the best buff type for a particular operation.

The most common buffs are bias-cut muslin. Their buffing performance is determined by thread count, number of piles and number of folds around the circumference. For the hard buffing or cutting operations, a wheel of high thread density (86-93) and large number of folds (No. 8 bias) might be used. For coloring a low thread density (64-68) and few folds (No. 2 bias) should be used.

Since heat is a problem in buffing aluminum, the buffs must be designed and constructed to dissipate heat rapidly. The color buffing wheel must have good shedding ability. That is, it must throw off metal particles and compound, otherwise the face will become "solid" and gouging will occur on the metal surface. The buffs must then be "raked" to remove the hard facing.
BUFFING PROBLEMS
Pitting

If the buffing compound is driven into the aluminum surface due to excessive pressure, a pit will result. The pit may not be apparent after buffing, or even after cleaning, but will show up after bright dipping.
Mottling

Elevated surface temperatures during buffing may be caused by excessive pressure, friction due to lack of lubrication, or hard buffs. Surface temperatures above 400°F / 204°C can cause metallurgical changes in the aluminum which appear in the anodized part as gray areas. No defect will be apparent until after bright dipping or anodizing.
Cloudiness

Areas on parts which have been "double" buffed, i.e., buffed more heavily than the rest of the part due to overlap in buffing from both directions, may appear cloudy after bright dipping. Cloudiness may also be due to inadequate or incomplete cleaning of the buffed surface. A compound which resists cleaning can be formed due to the reaction between aluminum and the stearates in the binder. This compound can be removed only in an etching bath, either an etching alkaline cleaner or a caustic etch.
CLEANING

Metal cleaning is a broad term covering the preparation of metal surfaces for an infinite variety of finishing processes, in the aluminum industry, a prerequisite for the success of nearly every finishing system is a clean surface. While the choice of the cleaning method for aluminum is 5 determined by a'number of factors, the most important considerations are: type of contaminant to be removed, surface condition required for subsequent finishing and size and shape of parts to be cleaned.

The soils prevalent on aluminum are usually fairly easy to remove. Because of the ease of working aluminum, drawing and machining lubricants need not be of the types that are very resistant to cleaning. The somewhat unique soil on aluminum sheet of marking inks and buffing compounds represents the most difficult soils to be removed. Several other contaminants are found. Among the 10 most common ones are oil, grease, wax or protective films remaining after rolling, drawing, extruding and fabricating operations. Shop dust, mill scale and metal oxides are some other contaminants that may also be present and must be taken into consideration.

Cleaning has been said to be the most common operation performed in the transformation of aluminum from raw metal to the finished product. Its importance, therefore, cannot be overemphasized. Many a costly anodizing job has been rejected because of improper or inadequate cleaning. Careful attention to cleaning will go a long way toward avoiding expensive rejections and 15 insuring a quality product.

The problems relating to the cleaning of aluminum are not simple, largely because of the sensitivity of the metal and its reactivity with many commonly used cleaners. Most aluminum finishers use alkaline cleaners or acid cleaners, separately or together in various combinations.
ALKALINE CLEANERS

2u Alkaline cleaners are used to remove drawing and stamping oils and buffing binders. They are also used where heavy soil loads are encountered. The cleaning ability of an alkaline cleaner comes from its ability to saponify fatty acids and fats and emulsify other oils and greases. Additives in the alkaline cleaners enable them to wet soils and to keep them suspended or dissolved.

Formulations of effective cleaners also contain water softeners which sequester or chelate calcium and magnesium salts in hard water to minimize the possibility of insoluble soap formation. They -,<- also contain buffering agents, which enable a cleaning solution to maintain a constant pH where its cleaning action is most effective.

Even mildly alkaline cleaners will attack aluminum, particularly at higher temperatures unless an inhibitor is present. Sometimes a slight, attack causes an etched appearance which is not objectionable, but is usually not desirable for bright work. Inhibitors are sometimes incorporated into the cleaner to reduce or prevent this etching in the cleaning stage. The most commonly used cleaner inhibitors, sodium silicate and sodium chromate, are not suitable for use on the bright
30 anodize line.

Silicated cleaners, operated in the pH range 11.3-11.7, protect the aluminum by forming a thin surface film. If this is not removed completely in hot cleaner rinses, upon entering any acid bath (an acid cleaner, bright dip or anodize bath), the silicate is converted to silicic acid which is insoluble. The insoluble silicic acid adheres to the parts and may cause pitting or an uneven streaked appearance.
Chromate inhibited cleaners are usually operated at a pH of 10 or less. They are not as effective
35 as silicate cleaners, and the chromate disposal problem has all but eliminated their use in anodizing.

Othercompounds may be used to give alkalinity and at the same time not be as harsh on the aluminum base metal. Such systems are preferred in the operation of the bright dip line to avoid the silicate contamination and chromate disposal problems. These other systems may contain sodium
carbonates, sodium phosphates, sodium metaborates or sodium tetraborate (borax). Frequently two or more these are blended together to maintain a reasonably high pH upon the addition of acid soils These may also be blended as buffers with sodium hydroxide to overcome the hygroscopic nature of sodium hydroxide and make for easier mixing and handling ACID CLEANERS

The maior advantages of using an acid cleaner are- (1 ) better metal oxide removal in an acid cleaner • these oxides include aluminum oxide and magnesium oxide which may be present due to in-plant corrosion or even rolled into the metal upon forming: (2) chloπnated and viscous paraffin oils are more easily emulsified in an acid cleaner - these oils are often used in the stamping and forming operations; (3) embedded buffing abrasives are more easily removed in an acid cleaner; (4) any other residues remaining after other cleaning operations are removed. The metal surface is termed "activated"; that is, the surface is free from any surface films and pure base metal is presented to the next operation The ideal cleaning cycle then should have, as a final cleaning step, an acid cleaner The acid cleaner could follow an alkaline cleaning stage or may be used by itself if the soil load is not too heavy
These types of acid cleaners are in use in the anodizing industry today:

( 1 ) Phosphoric acid cleaners like Albrrte 342-AC, 343-OC and 344-SC are superior for removing buffing compounds and metal oxides. In addition the surface is left "activated" or oxide free, which produces superior bnght work
(2) Sulfunc acid cleaners require inhibitors to prevent the parts from being deeply etched. Without tight control, parts may be dulled by these cleaners.

(3) Citric acid cleaners use a very mild acid as their base. They do not have the cleaning power of phosphoric acid cleaners, nor do they leave the surface etched or "activated" for further processing They are used m areas where phosphate restrictions prohibit the use of phosphoric acid cleaners.

CONTROL OF CLEANING BATHS

The chemical control of cleaning baths will vary with the type of cleaner and time allotted for laboratory control. These controls are usually supplied by the manufacturer of the chemicals and are based on extensive experience. c The tests usually used to analyze aluminum cleaners are as follows:
(1 ) Emulsion cleaners - break the emulsion with acid and measure the solvent separation.
(2) Etching, buffered alkaline cleaners and silicated cleaners - titrate with standard acid solutions.
(3) Acid cleaners - titrate with standard base.
(4) High detergent cleaners - detergent titrations, surface tension, acid-base titrations, cloud point Q determinations or surfactant analysis.
The control procedure used for each cleaner should be specified by the manufacturer of the cleaners.

"How long will a cleaner last?" is a common question. Since soil load, dragout of solution and type of soil are different for each operation, this is difficult to determine without a production test. Cleaners which etch usually require more maintenance than the non-etching cleaner. The qualify of the part produced and the number of rejects attributed to poor cleaning are the real measures 5 of a cleaner's value.

The simple water break test remains the most widely used method, in shop practice, to test for cleanliness. A cleaned metal panel, after being submerged in cold, clean, clear water, should show a continuous film of water over the entire surface. The presence of any residues will cause the water film to break, leaving those areas not wetted. Sometimes small areas will fail to show up immediately with this test, so sufficient time should be allowed to ensure that the film is continuous over the entire surface. 0

The preparation of metals for finishing is a most important consideration and, therefore, the cleaning operations require a considerable amount of planning. The appearance and acceptability of the finished article depends primarily on a sound cleaning process and clean foundation for the finish. A properly designed cycle will result in a quality part; likewise, an improper cleaning cycle will lead to rejects and higher costs. Therefore, the importance of proper cleaning cannot be overemphasized. 5
